b: Recently I wrote to the Moneyist on MarketWatch. You might want to read the full text.

“As a regular reader of The Moneyist, I am puzzled by letters from married couples that talk about his money and her money, her spending and his saving; he shares but she doesn’t, or vice versa; and money issues that seem to portray two people living separate financial lives, not a married couple, not ours, but yours and mine. I don’t get it.”

“To put that in perspective, I am 83 and we have been married for 58 years. My wife stopped working outside the home in 1970. In all those years, every money decision has been a joint one; every dollar has been ours; and bank and investment accounts are joint. We have never worried about each other overspending or incurring debt. Are we just abnormal, or is it a generational thing?”
The published answer started with:: “Yes. That’s the short answer. Now for the longer one.”
Now I know I am old and abnormal as a result.
Here is some more of what else the Moneyist said.

“People getting married today come with a lot more baggage — student debt, individual mortgages because they may have gotten married later in life and disparate credit scores — so separate accounts can protect the wealthier spouse. In the early days of your marriage, your money management was more tangible and a joint effort: You probably used checkbooks and cash together, drove to the supermarket together, and bought clothes in department stores together (or maybe you waited in the car).”

“Fair enough, but the other part of the story — your story — is not reflected in the research or statistics: luck and good fortune. You married the right woman, and she married the right man. You remained committed to your financial goals and true to your personal commitments. As a result, you divided the responsibility of raising and paying for a family, and paid for it as you went along. You are part of the tail end of the Silent Generation, so you know a thing or two about saving and being thrifty.”

“I hope you don’t mind me saying that you may have a slight “success bias” — your marriage lasted the test of time and you achieved a financially solid retirement. Many couples in your generation were not so lucky: They fought, they divorced, and they took what they could get from the marriage.”
I have admitted many times the absence of serious misfortune in our lives, but I refuse to accept that 58 years of marriage and financial prudence is just luck.
But I did marry the right woman.
